How about changing the tournament rules not to award any
VPs for reaching a time-out?

While at first glance it doesn't solve the main questions on
the tray (certain players making decks to win with time-outs
either with 2.5 VP in prelims or 0.5 VP in finals), it does
give a general boost to the willingness of players to move
forward.

Also, losing the incentive to "just hang in there and survive
for the 0.5 VP" might make for interesting new scenarios.

Of course we might need to revisit (eliminate?) the withdrawal
rule then.

Opinions?

--
Regards,

Daneel

Potential problem:

It doesn't look like I can oust my prey (both to me, observers and
judges.) Since I can't oust him, my possible VPs are maxed whether or
not I survive to the time limit or not.

Since it doesn't matter if I survive or not (in terms of playing to
win), I'm free to transfer myself out to my predator if I want, even
if he has no legitimate chance to oust me - I can just give him a VP
for the hell of it, and I'm still 'playing to win' by the tournament
rules.

And I'd think most players would not like a rules change that makes it
easier for people to legally 'transfer themselves out' or otherwise
deliberately throw VPs/games to their predator.

Signed.

I'm starting to dislike tournament games as they seem to are more and more
talking and "thinking" and less and less about playing the game.

Some examples from my latest:

* Looking at your hand 10 times when you KNOW you don't have a deflection
while pretending to be contemplating wheter or not to bounce is not good
play. Looking once, maybe twice and pondering it for 20-25 seconds - sure.
Anything more is stalling.

* Thinking for 5 minutes before you do that hunt action, pretending to have
some masterplan in mind doesn't make you intimidating and strong. At best it
looks like you're stalling; at worst you annoy the other 4 players.

* When you're tapped out with no wakes in hand, 1 pool with one minute on
the clock while your opponent bleeds you, means you're ousted. No amount of
staring at your hand faking you're thinking about which minion to wake while
waiting for the time to run out is going to save your ass. It's bad
sportmanship if not plain cheating.

* Putting a card face-down on the table when someone is being
Conditioning-ousted pretending it's a DI is to see the effect one thing.
Taking 7-8 minute to negotiate a deal with your predator (who was being
ousted) and then taking the card back saying: "nah you'll break it anyway"
is a whole different thing especially if the card turns out not to be a DI
and you're next to get ousted unless that clock runs out (which it thank god
did just AFTER you got ousted...)

I don't think zero VP for a time-out isn't a good idea for reasons mentioned
above among others. I'd like to see a 30-minute per player time limit and
just play with a 5-way chess clock (these actually exist, yes) and still
time at 2 hours. If it runs out you're out as well - Your predator gains 1
VP and six pool. Thanks for playing - next time play faster and play your
Deck instead of Diplomacy.

Solved.

And don't get me started on 'decks that take long turns'. Any decent player
can handle 12-13 turns in 30 minutes with ANY deck and have time spare for
some talk.

What it comes down to is resource management. You have a limited
resource in a finals which is a time limit. It is not alloted equally
to all players but apportioned according to use. Therefore, the first
place player can "politic", stall, play-slow, play Imbued, or any
other manner to burn up the clock which doesn't get him in trouble
with the judge. This according to LSJ is playing to win.

It is unsportmanlike behavior that goes against the intent of the
game.

As I have allready complained many times the game design does have a too
strong favor for reactive cards for my taste (for the last few
expansions). A lot of new intercept possibilities emerged (Bowl of
Convergence, many locations, Unmasking ...) but only very little (good)
stuff to push actions through (Veil of the Legions, perhaps Vermin Channel).

requirements, is a bleed for +2 at +5 stealth, most likely no game would
time out. Obviously this is not a well designed card but it shows the
point: Game Design needs to put more focus on taking resources *off* the
table instead of protecting them or getting them back.

Huh what?

Going backwards, here's EVERY new library card that provides
intercept:

Sword of Caine: Number of new intercept cards: 1 (Census Taker).
Third edition: Number of new intercept cards: 1 (Abbot.)
(Nights of Reckoning: No intercept cards that can be used by non-
imbued.)
Legacies of Blood: 6 cards. (Ahriman Protectorate, No Secrets,
Predator's Communion, Quicksilver Contemplation, Scry the Hearthstone,
Shaman.)
Kindred Most Wanted: 6: (Anima Gathering, Bloodstone, Harzomatuili,
Phased Motion Detector, Trophy: Domain, Warning Sirens.)
10th Anniversary: 3 cards. Bowl of Convergence, Channel 10, Carlton
Van Wyck.
Gehenna: 4 cards. Instinctive Reaction, Divine Sign, Friend of Mine,
The Unmasking.
Promos: 1. (Wall Street)

So in the last SEVEN expansions, or three years, we've seen a grand
total of twenty-two new intercept cards (plus NoR's imbued-specific
stuff.)

Of those 22 cards, maybe nine actually see regular play. At least
seven of them are rarely if ever played (Divine Sign, Warning Sirens,
PMD, Quicksilver, Protectorate, Bloodstone, Harzo).

So by "Many locations", you mean... two?

Want to take a wild guess at how many new cards in that time period
provide stealth or inhibit someone's ability to block (not even
counting inherent-stealth actions)? It's a _lot_ more than the 9
intercept cards regularly played, or the 15 even played occasionally,
or even the 22 total printed in the last 3 years.

In fact, I'd argue that since KMW came out, there's been a near
absolute -lack-
of new intercept options, not an unbalancing and unending stream of
them.

more reactively and defensively instead of ousting their prey.

Which is a reasonable statement--except that the game design has been
trying to catch up every other strategy to compete with Stealth and
Bleed since day 1. All of the increases in defense that have fallen into
the game in the last 10 years are likely the direct result of Stealth
and Bleed being too good from day 1, and the rest of the game trying to
compete effectively.

necessary function to make non S+B strategies viable. But in doing so,
the rest of the game (that isn't S+B) is forced to slow down a lot.
Which leads to slow game.

Endless table talk certainly doesn't help, though.

On Aug 28, 12:37 pm, Daneel <dan...@eposta.hu> wrote:
> How about changing the tournament rules not to award any
> VPs for reaching a time-out?
>

> While at first glance it doesn't solve the main questions on
> the tray (certain players making decks to win with time-outs
> either with 2.5 VP in prelims or 0.5 VP in finals), it does
> give a general boost to the willingness of players to move
> forward.
>
> Also, losing the incentive to "just hang in there and survive
> for the 0.5 VP" might make for interesting new scenarios.

I assume you also intend to remove the draw rules as well?

I think it's important to have the 0.5 VPs available for those who
hang on. I'm not encouraging stalling, but having that 0.5 VP carrot
keeps things in balance.

With 0 VPs for a timeout, if I'm at a table that's going to time out,
I can simply self-oust or go entirely crosstable. I'm going to get 0
VPs anyway, so it becomes PTW for me to kingmake.

One of the most destructive (and least fun) aspects of the game is
kingmaking when someone is in a completely lost position. If we
remove the 0.5 VPs from a timeout, then we increase such kingmaking.

It sounds like your real concern is that tables time out, and that's
not fun or desirable. In tournament standings, it's so important to
get GWs that I feel like most good players push for the GW. That
said, sometimes it's best to just take it slow. I think that's simply
the nature of a 5 player game, and we'll never be rid of that
entirely.

In the finals, the lower seeds have the responsibility to move the
game forward. I personally haven't seen intentional stalling on the
part of the 1st seed, but I'm willing to admit it might happen.

Also, from a fun perspective, I've played plenty of fun games that
have timed out.

Govern and Conditioning went, we'd probably have to get all the cards
that let you bleed for +2 with an inferior discipline.

Would just make the game all around better and easier to play.

-Protect Thine Own

Still the most broken card in the game.

And moved on from there, I think VTES would be much, much better all
around. Memories is also a possibility, but only, really, 'cause of the
Imbued, and I'd still just rather see the Imbued get fixed on the rules
front rather than on the card or card text front.

such blanket effects are, well, unknown but for a single card, makes it

possibility to DIing whatever card just got played. And any time anyone
tries to do anything at a table, someone can say "Wait, I might want to

for everyone.

introduced into the game. Ever.

hypothetical sense, to make the game as a whole a better* place for
everyone", DI is likely on the top of the list.

(*by "better", I mean "better balanced, more fun, and more varied in
terms of viable strategies".)

I didn't follow the discussions at this forum for some days so excuse

Apparently dominate is the discipline of choice for many players
playing at tournaments. Some guys proved that already by looking at
the TWA.
We all agree that dominate is one of the most useful disciplines at
the moment because of the mentioned cards above.
In my opinion this is true not because of game mechanics or mistakes
at game design in the past but because of the fact, that people tend
to play specific decktypes at today tournaments. You can be enormously
successful by playing those decks.

If you want to change that you don't have to alter cards or rules. You
have to adjust your playstyle.

If you are annoyed by decks relying heavy on deflections and bleed
cards play decks which can hit them (i.e. combat decks). Dominate
relying decks are seldom good at combat defence. If I have to fear
hitting decks at tourneys I cannot participate with decks completely
without combat defence like I can today. If I have to worry about
combat, I have to add cards. With that I lose focus. And that leads to
that bigger variation of decks at tournaments we like to see.
At the moment people learned what decks are the most useful in today's
metagame. This problem can be solved by playing decks which can
counter them and thus changing the metagame. The problem cannot be
solved by banning cards or tuning down bleeddecks (really guys, I
can't believe what I just read in this thread).

If I play a bleed deck in my playgroup in Frankfurt I often get hit
from Enkidu, weenie to midcap potence, guns, War Ghouls and so on. In
that environment no dominate deck can win. So changing that
environment is the key, not changing deck-archetypes.

I know that many players now yell "how should I get into finals with a
frikking combatdeck"? True, combat decks don't often get sweeps or
high GWs. But if you hinder those monster-sweep-decks to win you don't
need high stats for finals anymore. And a good combat deck is capable
to get a 2-3 VP GW at any table.

If you want to work on a weakness of the game do something about the
weenies.

If players perceive a metagame shift against such decks (if nothing
else, enhanced table hate), this number may pre-emptively go down. If
everyone is going to hate you and you can't deal well with managing a
whole table full of hate and defence and thumping, you play a different
deck. The metagame has its effect without being seen in the way you
seem to want.

>point me to the defence that the final decks had against them.

If the metagame shifts against a deck style, as is being claimed,
individual decks don't have to and may, in fact, thrive by not devoting
card-space to counter a threat that the rest of the table will shut
down. For example, if your bogeyman deck was Imbued and the metagame
shifted against it, a player may do better by not including specific
anti-Imbued defence because he can reasonably rely on other people on
the table doing that for him. (For example, his grand-predator might
eat the Imbued deck with Smiling Jack.) This may not always be a
conscious effort, of course.

Over the whole tournament, the design choices of the non-finalists (i.e.
the majority of players in most tournaments) can, in some ways, reverse
king-make who /doesn't/ make the final. This is no surprise to anyone
who's seen a shifting metagame. Combat is a problem. So everyone plays
combat defence, so combat decks have a way harder time winning games or
making finals. So then some average or better player(s) decides "Fuck
that, no-one is going to play combat around here anymore" and decides to
play little to no combat defence, and uses the 20 cards saved to kick
some ass. And so the metagame can shift to react to that brutally
effective weenie vote deck that's just been created, or whatever.

That finalists don't have particular defences against particular deck
styles won't, therefore, necessarily prove a whole lot. It can
certainly be interesting to see, but it's not going to definitely be
significant.

proposed a variation on this many years ago. Something like this:

"A vampire may neither bleed, not cast votes, nor singly strike for
damage in excess of its capacity."

very strong).

One of the attractive aspects of the NWO VTES I suggested is, at least
for me, that it doesn't actually change the game all that much. Which is
good, as, well, I like the way the game works currently, for the most
part. But there are still a few cards that are at the top of the power
curve by a considerable margin (the ones I suggest killing). Getting rid
of these would change the game in a subtle way (making it harder to
bleed for huge amounts, making non camarilla vampires safer to play,
making bounce a little harder to get, and just, ya know, getting rid of
DI) without doing untold collateral damage.

Most of those were discussed in this thread. My view is, at least, not
necessarily killing all bleeds of 6+, but making them harder to get
ahold of *and* making Dominate, specifically, less good. Govern and
Conditioning are the obvious power bleed cards. Legal Manipulations
probably needs to go too if Govern goes. But the rest of the cards
mentioned have a great deal to make them much less of an issue:

-Aire is less good than Threats if you aren't a Toreador, and if you are
a Toreador, you have very limited delivery capabilities (i.e. no
reliable stealth). So reasonable.

-Command the Beast: Requires an extra card and DOM to get the extra +1
bleed. Reasonable. Currently, Command the Beast is mostly wallpaper, as
the effort for the extra +1 bleed isn't generally worth it. With Govern
and Conditioning gone, Command suddenly becomes an attractive and
powerful card. Which is a nice effect of what I suggest.

-Force of Will: Very significant cost (minimum of 2 blood and a trip to
torpor).

-Iron Glare: Only gives you +2 bleed with POT/PRE. And as such is less
good than Threats.

-Madman's Quill: Teetering on the edge of being in the same spot as
Govern, but at least requires aus as well as dem, which isn't completely
insignificant. And the superior is mostly useless.

-Sense the Sin: Requires a superior discipline. And, generally speaking,
being infernal. Reasonable.

-Slaughtering the Herd: Costs 2 blood. Superior is kind of a waste. As a
plus, specifically hoses the Imbued.

-Truth: Costs 2 blood.

Again, my intention is not to completely destroy bleeding as a strategy.
Or even limit it to a maximum of 5. Just to make it harder to bleed for
a lot (given the suggestions I have, it is generally difficult to bleed
for more than 3 with an inferior discipline--with dom, you can bleed for
maximum of 4 for 2 blood, and this is only if you are playing with
Slaughtering the Herd; with pre, you can bleed for 4 for 2 blood with
Legal and Aire, *if* you are a Toreador and Legal is still in play) and
power down Dominate across the board.

without weenies, and weenies can exist without causing this problem,
then why exactly are you singling out weenies, when it's obviously
decks that are one-minded about ruining their prey that cause the
problem?

enough to be changed is because they don't actually work. And when
people go into a real competitive tournament, they tend to play things
with a track record -- something that has worked consistently in the
past. And while weenies seem to do well in some smaller tournaments
and amongst inexperienced and/or intercept light playgroups, they

problems there.

Assamites and preemptive rush decks are bad, whether anyone at the
table influences weenies or not. It's an entirely unrelated problem.
Making weenies less powerful will not result in previously bad decks
suddenly being good. I apologize for my hyberbole, which I didn't
recognize until you pointed it out. I meant that all the traditional
(non-joke) deck types -- voters, blockers, stealth-bleeders, etc. --
are still racking up tournament wins, just like they were in 1997.
Except that intercept decks are getting more wins, probably thanks to
the GW rule, and weenies are getting less.

Now I'm wondering about the data, though. Maybe one of you Perl
wizards could find some quick way to summarize average capacity of the
TWDA's decks categorized by year, or some such. :)

In summary, I don't think weenies always cripple their first prey. I
don't think weenies are the only way to cripple your prey. I don't
think weenies are nearly as effective as they once were, and I don't
think unsuccessful decks will get picked consistently for competitive
play. Therefore, competitive play doesn't really have a "weenie
problem". There was a while that AUS was strong, with or without
weenies. There was a time that clans with a way to double their bleed
did great with weenies. And there was a time, long, long ago, when
just using weenies with dominate or Legacy of Pander was very strong,
but I feel all of these times are behind us, based on my experiences
in competitive play, and supported by what little data is available.

-- Brian

Because every other strategy has been boosted.

- Defensive decks now have Aranthebes, No Secrets from the Magaji,
Carlton Van Wyk, Bowl of Convergence, and more vampires than ever with
inherent +1 intercept. Perhaps most importantly, they have the GW
rule.

- Voters have appeared in record numbers, partly due to larger
vampires getting more and more for their capacity than they ever have
before. This happens to make weenie vote exceptionally hard to pull
off, compared to 5 years ago.

- Aggressive midcap decks have to compensate for the increase in
intercept, and consequently, Elder Impersonation, Call of the Hungry
Dead, Pentex Subversion, Mind Numb, Aching Beauty, and Toreador Grand
Ball have started being regulars on the tournament scene--some of
which aren't useful with smaller vamps at all.

- And lastly, but still very important, there now exist the Imbued.
Play weenie bleed and sit behind Imbued, and you die. Every time.

of. I know they've LOST Anarch Revolt, free basic Majesty, and the
discipline card for The Embrace. I don't know when Legacy of Pander

I don't know whether I feel more strongly that the game should not be
able to be over before you can act, or that a deck without defense
should expect to die. I already accept that a deck without offense
will probably time out, so why shouldn't I accept that a deck with no
defense will die?

offense by the game's nature, so decks should realistically include

weenies from ruining your game in most cases, especially as they
continue to print new cards that make that task easier. NUN etc.
